---
# The Dignity of the Lighthouse

I have never lived near a lighthouse, and I have visited only a few. Still, I think about them often, the way one thinks about a distant relative who did something unusual with their life. A lighthouse is a strange kind of building. It has no purpose except to say, over and over, in the dark: *here is the danger, and here is where you are not.* It is a tower built to prevent one specific kind of sorrow.

What I want to do here is wander around the idea, which is not quite a history or an argument. I want to look at why these structures have a hold on us, and what it means that most of them are now obsolete.

## A Man Who Wished for a Storm

Start with Henry Winstanley, who in 1698 began building a lighthouse on the Eddystone Rocks, a reef about fourteen miles off Plymouth, England. The rocks were notorious. They lay just below the surface, in the path of ships entering the English Channel, and they had wrecked vessel after vessel. Winstanley was not a builder by training. He was an engineer of amusements, a man who had made a house of trick mechanisms and a "Water Theatre" that dazzled paying visitors. It was an odd résumé for someone tackling one of the most violent stretches of water in Britain.

His tower was, by all accounts, fanciful. It had ornamental flourishes, a wide lantern, and candles for light. The sea battered it in the first year, and he rebuilt it larger and sturdier. It stood for about five years and did its work. Then, in November 1703, Winstanley went out to make repairs. He is supposed to have said that he wished to be inside his lighthouse during the worst storm that ever blew, so that he could see how it would stand.

He got his wish. The Great Storm of 1703 remains one of the most severe ever recorded in Britain. In the morning there was nothing on the rock but a few twisted iron fragments. Winstanley and the men with him were gone.

The story is usually told as a parable of hubris, but I read it differently. Winstanley's wish sounds less like arrogance than like faith, the kind that makes people build things they know the ocean might take back. Every lighthouse is a bet against the sea, and the sea does not lose often, or for long. The first of these structures were built by people who understood they were wagering against something that would eventually collect. They built anyway, because the alternative was to let the ships keep dying.

## The Oak and the Granite

The story improves with the next builder. After the second tower burned down in 1755 (it was made of wood, and a fire started in the lantern), the job went to John Smeaton, an engineer who had made his name with mills and water wheels. Smeaton did something clever: he studied the oak tree.

An oak, he noticed, is broad at the base and narrows as it rises, and it bends in the wind without breaking. It also grips the ground with roots that spread wide. He designed his tower with the same curve, a flared base sweeping up into a slender column. He also invented a form of hydraulic lime, a cement that would set underwater, which became foundational to modern concrete. And he cut the granite blocks so they interlocked with dovetail joints, like a puzzle, so that each stone was held in place by its neighbors as well as by mortar.

Smeaton's Tower was completed in 1759 and lit for almost 120 years. It was eventually taken down not because it failed but because the rock beneath it was being undermined by the waves. The upper part was carried to Plymouth Hoe, where it stands today as a monument. The base remains on the reef, a stump beside its towering successor.

I find this moving in a quiet way. Smeaton did not conquer the sea. He *listened* to a tree, and so he built something that worked with the forces trying to destroy it. There is a lesson in that beyond engineering, about resistance versus flexibility, but I distrust morals that come too neatly. What I will say is that the best lighthouses are more than defiance. They are negotiations.

## The Lens

The next great leap wasn't in stone but in glass. In the early 1820s, a French physicist named Augustin-Jean Fresnel worked out how to make a lens that could project a beam of extraordinary power without the ridiculous thickness a conventional lens of that size would require.

The problem was this: to focus light from a flame into a strong horizontal beam, you need a big lens, and a big convex lens is a thick, heavy, light-absorbing lump of glass. Fresnel's insight was to slice the lens into concentric rings and keep only the parts that actually bend the light, discarding the bulk in between. What resulted was a lens made of stepped prisms arranged in a beehive shape, thin and light, that captured almost all of the light from the lamp and threw it out in a concentrated beam. Around the central lens, additional rings of prisms caught the light that would have escaped above and below and bent it back into the beam.

The result was startling. A single lamp inside a Fresnel lens could be seen many miles farther than the same lamp behind older reflectors. Some of the largest lenses, the "hyperradiant" ones, stand taller than a person and look like enormous crystalline hives, glinting with hundreds of hand-ground prisms. They are among the most beautiful objects that the age of industry produced, and they were made for a purpose with no vanity in it at all.

Fresnel died in 1827, at thirty-nine, of tuberculosis. He lived to see his lenses begin to be installed but not to see them become the standard around the world. I think of him sometimes when I think about how much of what protects us was made by people who never saw the full effect of their work. Fresnel saved more lives than he could have counted, and never got to count.

## The Keepers

A lighthouse is not only its light, though. For most of their history these places were inhabited, and the keepers may be the most interesting part of the story.

Consider the peculiar job description. You live in a tower on a rock, or on a lonely headland, or on a spit of sand. You keep the light burning. That means trimming wicks, polishing brass, cleaning lenses, winding clockwork mechanisms that rotated the lens, hauling oil, and keeping a log. If fog came, you sounded the horn or rang the bell, sometimes for days on end. You did this in shifts, with other men, or with your family, or, in a few lonely stations, mostly by yourself.

The reality was a mix of tedium and terror. Long stretches of routine were interrupted by storms that could shake the tower and strand the crew, or by rescues in which keepers rowed out to wrecks. Keepers were expected to be self-sufficient, orderly, and calm. Many of them kept meticulous journals, and reading them is a strange pleasure. The entries are often dull on purpose: *wind NW, moderate; lamp lit at 4:15; nothing sighted.* But between the lines lies a discipline of attention. Somebody stayed awake so that somebody else, unknown to them, could sleep.

The most famous lighthouse story involves keepers who vanished. In December 1900, three men disappeared from the Flannan Isles lighthouse, in the Outer Hebrides. When a relief ship arrived, the station was empty. The clocks had stopped, or so the legend goes, and a chair had been overturned, and there were oilskins missing from the pegs. The truth is probably less eerie than the legend. The most likely explanation is that a freak wave swept the men from a landing area as they were securing equipment during a storm. The log entries that supposedly described strange weather and the men praying were later inventions, embellishments from ballads and stories. But the fact that the story stuck says something about how we imagine these places. We picture them as thresholds, spots where the ordinary world thins and something else looks through.

## Automation and the Quiet

Today almost all lighthouses are automated. In Scotland, the last manned lighthouse, on Fair Isle, was automated in 1998. In the United States, Boston Light, the country's oldest lighthouse station, is the only one that still has resident keepers, kept on by an act of Congress as a matter of heritage. Elsewhere, the beacons run on sensors and solar panels, checked by technicians on periodic visits. The lenses were often replaced with LED beacons no larger than a bucket.

And in one sense that is simply progress. Nobody should be required to live for months on a wave-swept rock if a machine can do the job. The keepers' lives were hard, and the romance we attach to them is partly the romance of distance. Still, something has gone quiet. A human being was once the guarantor of the light, and now a circuit is.

And then there's the larger matter that most ships no longer need lighthouses, or not in the way they once did. GPS tells a captain where the vessel is to within a few meters. Radar sees the coastline in fog. Electronic charts display every known hazard. The lighthouse, once the pinnacle of maritime safety, has become a backup, a redundancy, and in many places a tourist attraction, an Instagram backdrop, or a seaside museum. Some have been converted into inns. Some are simply left to crumble.

I keep thinking about the word "obsolete," and about how strange it is. It suggests something whose purpose has been taken over by something better. But a thing can be obsolete and still be *right*, in the sense that it embodies a certain relationship between people and the world that we should not entirely lose.

## What a Lighthouse Knows

Let me try to say what I think that relationship is.

A lighthouse is a form of care that is both impersonal and specific. It is impersonal because it doesn't know who is out there. It shines for the fishing boat, the freighter, and the yacht in the same way, and for the sailor who is grateful and the one who never glances up. It is specific because it is tied to one place. It says the same thing every night: *this coast, this rock, this hazard.* There is no generic lighthouse. Each has its own signature, its own pattern of flashes, so that a sailor can identify it, one flash every ten seconds here, two flashes every twenty there. Each is a small sentence spoken in a private language shared between a place and everyone who has ever needed to know it.

I find that pairing wonderful: indiscriminate generosity anchored to a particular spot. It is what we admire in a good teacher, a good doctor, or a good neighbor, someone whose care doesn't depend on whether you deserve it, and who nevertheless knows the local terrain. Most of what keeps a society running is like this, quiet infrastructure. Levees, water mains, and the people who check the smoke detectors. Nobody notices when it works. A lighthouse is unusual only in that it made its service visible, turning it into a beam sweeping over the water.

There is also something to be said for the honesty of the design. A lighthouse can't be subtle or disguised. Its whole function is to be conspicuous, and to be conspicuous about *danger*. That is almost the opposite of how we tend to behave. Most of us hide our hazards and advertise our attractions. The lighthouse advertises the hazard. It stands right at the edge of the thing that could kill you and says, *look here.* It is a building made of warning, and yet we experience it as comfort. That's a remarkable psychological fact. To see the light in a storm is to know that someone, at some point, thought about you and did something about it.

## The Argument for Keeping Them

People argue about whether old lighthouses deserve preservation. The practical case is thin. They cost money, they are exposed to brutal weather, and their original job has largely disappeared. Yet preservation societies flourish, volunteers repaint towers, and communities fight to save structures that no ship depends on.

I think the impulse is right, though not for the reasons usually offered. It isn't simply nostalgia, and it isn't only architectural appreciation. We keep lighthouses because they are *evidence*, physical proof that people once organized themselves around the principle that a stranger's life was worth a great deal of effort. Someone hauled granite to a rock in the open ocean for the sake of people they would never meet. That is not a trivial thing to have on record. It is a data point about what humans can be, and it is good to have such data points standing where we can see them, especially when other data points suggest otherwise.

There is also value in the fact that a lighthouse is legible. You can look at one and understand its whole purpose in a moment. Few things in modern life are like that. My phone contains billions of components, and I understand almost none of them. A lighthouse is a tall thing with a light on top, put there to keep boats off the rocks. It is a whole ethic in a single sentence.

## The Last Image

I'll end with an image, since lighthouses are really images before they are anything else.

Picture a coast at night. The sea is black and the sky is only slightly less so. Somewhere out on the water, a ship is moving, its crew tired, its route half-remembered, its instruments possibly working and possibly not. Far ahead, low on the horizon, a small point of light appears, vanishes, appears again. It keeps to a rhythm. Someone on the bridge counts the seconds, checks a chart, and says quietly, *there she is.*

That moment, the recognition of a known signal in a big dark, is one of the oldest human comforts. We do it with stars, with campfires, with a lit window seen from a road. The lighthouse just formalized the idea and gave it stone legs.

Technology will keep changing how we navigate, and the towers will keep getting quieter. Perhaps one day none will be lit at all. But I hope we don't forget what they were doing, which was telling strangers the truth, at a cost, on a schedule, without asking for anything back. If we can manage to build more of our world in that spirit, then a lot of the lighthouses' work will go on, even after the last lamp goes dark.
---
